cues.text: Chapter three is about industry disruption.
We begin with the central idea.
Technological disruption changes established patterns of competition and value creation.
In other words, it changes who competes, how they compete, and where the value in an industry is actually created and captured.
Where does disruption come from?
The source gives several origins.
It may arise from lower costs, from new delivery channels, from new customer groups, from business-model shifts, or from rapid improvements in capabilities.
Let us take these one at a time.
Lower costs means a new approach lets someone serve customers at a price the old approach cannot match.
A new delivery channel means the product reaches customers by a different route.
New customer groups means people who were previously not served, or poorly served, now become buyers.
A business-model shift means the way money is earned changes, for example from selling a product once to charging for access.
And rapid improvements in capabilities means a technology gets better so quickly that it can do things it could not do before.
Now we come to an important distinction.
Sustaining innovations improve an existing offering.
They make a current product or service better for the customers it already serves.
Disruptive innovations are different.
They can initially serve overlooked needs, meaning needs that established firms were ignoring or treating as unimportant, and later they can challenge incumbents.
An incumbent is simply an established firm that already holds a strong position in the market.
So the pattern is this: the disruptor starts at the edges, with needs the leaders overlook, and then grows until it threatens the leaders.
This leads to a caution that the source states directly.
Adding a minor digital feature is not necessarily industry disruption.
If a bank adds a small new option to its existing app, or a shop adds a button to its website, that may well be a sustaining improvement.
To call something disruption, we should look for a real change in competition and value creation, not just the presence of technology.
Let us now look at the examples the source offers.
First, streaming changes media distribution and rental economics.
The way media reaches people changes, and so does the economics of renting it.
Second, fintech services expand access and challenge traditional financial intermediaries.
Fintech means financial technology, and an intermediary is a party that sits between two sides of a transaction, such as a traditional bank between savers and borrowers.
Fintech widens access to financial services and puts pressure on those established intermediaries.
Third, ride-hailing platforms change transport coordination.
They change how riders and drivers find and organise trips with one another.
Fourth, cloud computing shifts infrastructure purchasing toward on-demand services.
Instead of buying and owning computing infrastructure in advance, organisations can obtain what they need when they need it.
The source adds two qualifications that we must keep.
Some incumbents adapt successfully, so disruption does not mean the established firm always loses.
And new entrants can fail, so being new and digital does not guarantee success.
These examples illustrate patterns; they are not proof that every disruptor wins.
Next, how do we identify disruption before it overwhelms us?
The source lists several approaches.
First, customer feedback, which shows unmet or changing needs.
Second, trend scanning, which means systematically watching for developments in the wider environment.
Third, competitor analysis, which means studying what existing and new rivals are doing.
Fourth, technology maturity, which asks how ready and reliable a technology is becoming.
Fifth, weak signals, which are early, faint hints of change that are easy to dismiss.
Sixth, emerging regulation, because new rules can open or close opportunities.
Seventh, business-model changes, which means noticing when others earn revenue in new ways.
And eighth, changing unit economics, which means the cost and revenue of serving a single customer or transaction are shifting.
Once disruption is identified, how should an organisation respond?
The source lists these responses: experiments, partnerships, capability-building, investment diversification, strategic pivots, and controlled cannibalisation of legacy offerings.
Experiments let you learn cheaply before committing heavily.
Partnerships bring in capabilities or access that you lack.
Capability-building develops your own skills and resources.
Investment diversification spreads your bets across more than one possible future.
A strategic pivot is a deliberate change of direction.
And controlled cannibalisation means you deliberately allow your new offering to take sales from your own older offering, in a managed way, rather than letting a competitor do it for you.
That brings us to a well-known trap, the innovator's dilemma.
The source puts it this way: protecting present revenues can block the future model.
A firm that clings to the income from its current products may refuse to build the new model that will replace them, and so it is overtaken.
The advice is to avoid this trap.
Finally, the source introduces scenario planning.
Scenario planning considers multiple plausible futures rather than treating one forecast as certainty.
Instead of betting everything on a single prediction, the organisation imagines several believable ways the future could unfold, and prepares for each.
This keeps strategy flexible when the direction of change is uncertain.

To bring the chapter together: disruption changes competition and value creation; it must be distinguished from sustaining innovation; it is detected through many signals; it is answered through experiments, partnerships, capability-building, diversification, pivots and controlled cannibalisation;
and it is guarded against by avoiding the innovator's dilemma and by planning for more than one future.
